Diagnosis: the observed failure is PROGRAM_NOT_JSON: duplicate key: do — a wire-encoding defect, not a semantic one. The serialized program object for the outer let (the node binding uniq, and the analogous pattern near the stock map) contains two sibling "do" fields at the same object level, which is illegal JSON; most parsers reject the document before any expression evaluates. No case ran, so the evidence is blocked at parse time. Per the ground rules an interpreter error is a construction/translation failure, so I do not treat it as a refutation of the prose. I also do not accept the prose as verified; the account is unresolved at the execution layer until it parses and runs.

Operative change: re-encode the same algorithm as strictly valid JSON, with exactly one "do" per let node and no duplicated sibling keys, and fix the substantive latent defect carried over from the candidate: the malformed object had "do" binding the reserved_for let but the available field was an incomplete call to max_by (a {"value":[block]}-like structure with no name/name key), which would itself be an evaluation error even after the parse is fixed. The repair is causal and minimal: (a) legal JSON — every object uses distinct keys, each let carries exactly one value and one do; (b) compute capacity per item as the single stock row's capacity via max_by/min_by over the one-item filter, not as an unmotivated get on a list; (c) delete the unused reserved_for binding entirely since reserved is computed inline in the output object; (d) keep the algorithm identical: unique(deliveries) -> group by booking -> max_by revision -> keep latest holds with expires_at > now -> sum quantity per item -> sorted item rows with available = capacity - reserved, unclamped.

Why this addresses the actual failure: the only demonstrated failure is the duplicate "do" key, which is a serialization bug. The repair makes the document valid JSON so evaluation can begin, and the capacity fix removes the second, independent execution error that would surface next. Neither change alters the mechanism, so the prose's claims remain testable rather than replaced.

Preserved previously successful behavior: structural deduplication of repeated deliveries contributes once; the greatest integer revision is authoritative and replaces all lower revisions regardless of delivery order; a latest release contributes 0; an expired latest hold contributes 0 and does not resurrect an older hold; per-item reserved is the sum of active latest quantities; every stock item appears in ascending name order; available = capacity - reserved may be negative (no clamping, no discard, no invented rejection order).

Assumptions: revision, quantity, capacity, expires_at, now are integers; each booking maps to exactly one item; events name listed stock items; a booking/revision pair never carries conflicting contents. Falsifiers: if any two delivered records with equal booking and revision differed in content, the max_by tie-break (first wins) would silently pick one — that would defeat the account; if a booking named an unlisted item, the item row set would be incomplete; if a release could carry a lower revision than a later hold, latest-wins would misclassify. None of these are granted by the task, but they mark the account's boundary. Discriminating case: booking b, rev 1 hold qty 5 expires_at 20, rev 2 hold qty 2 expires_at 5, now=10, capacity 10 — delivery-order or incremental-delta readings give 5 or 7 reserved; the intended account gives reserved 0, available 10. Any future revision must preserve greatest-revision authority and once-only contribution of a duplicated immutable record.

answer.body: The obligations define a fold over an unordered, duplicating delivery stream whose final state depends only on booking identity, revision, and time. The mechanism is: (1) deduplicate deliveries structurally, because identical immutable records carry no new information; (2) group by booking; (3) within each booking choose the greatest revision, breaking no ties because a booking/revision pair never conflicts; (4) classify only that latest revision: a release contributes 0, a hold contributes quantity only if expires_at > now, otherwise 0; (5) sum those contributions per item; (6) emit every stock row sorted by item, with available = capacity - reserved, allowing negative availability. Replay and reordering are harmless because the result is a function of the set of (booking, revision) records, not their delivery order; duplicate delivery is absorbed by structural deduplication. Expiry is a predicate on the latest revision's expires_at against input.now, so an expired hold vanishes entirely and cannot resurrect an older hold. Later cancellation works because a release is a strictly higher integer revision for the same booking, so it replaces all lower holds and contributes zero. Oversubscription is never clamped or filtered: reserved can exceed capacity and available becomes negative, which is the observable signal. The procedure assumes revision numbers are comparable integers, each booking has exactly one item, events name listed stock items, and no booking/revision pair carries contradictory content; an event for an unlisted item would make the account incomplete rather than falsify it, since the task guarantees events name listed items. A discriminating failure case is: booking b has revision 1 hold quantity 5 expires_at 20 and revision 2 hold quantity 2 expires_at 5, with now=10 and capacity 10. A delivery-order or incremental-delta implementation might count 5 or 5+2; the correct account discards revision 1, sees the latest hold expired, reserves 0, and reports available 10. Any revision of this program must preserve that the latest revision by integer order is authoritative and that duplicate delivery of the same record contributes once. The program is a direct expression of these steps using group-like selection via max_by, so it is not a lookup of the public examples.
